questions.content:
Question 1: Coastal wind farm

A wind farm has 24 identical turbines. Each turbine has a rated power of 2.5 megawatts (MW). Over a full year the farm produces, on average, 35% of its rated total power. The farm cost £96 million to build. The cost is split between turbines, installation and grid connection in the ratio 7 : 4 : 1. An average household uses electricity at a constant rate of 0.5 kilowatts (kW). 1 MW = 1000 kW = 1 000 000 W.

(a) Calculate the total rated power of the wind farm in MW. (1 mark)
(b) Write your answer to (a) in watts, in standard form. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the average power produced by the wind farm over a year. (2 marks)
(d) Determine how many households the average power could supply. (2 marks)
(e) Calculate the amount spent on the turbines. (2 marks)
(f) Estimate the energy produced in a year of 8760 hours. Give your answer in gigawatt-hours (GWh), correct to 3 significant figures. (1 GWh = 1000 MWh) (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] 24 × 2.5 = 60 MW
(b)
[1] 6 × 10⁷ W. ECF from (a) if the answer is in correct standard form.
(c)
[1] Method: 35% of 60, i.e. 0.35 × 60
[1] 21 MW. ECF from (a).
Common error: using 35% of 2.5 only (8.75 MW).
(d)
[1] Unit conversion: 21 MW = 21 000 kW
[1] 21 000 ÷ 0.5 = 42 000 households. ECF from (c).
Common error: not converting MW to kW, giving 42.
(e)
[1] Total parts = 7 + 4 + 1 = 12, so 1 part = £96 million ÷ 12 = £8 million
[1] Turbines = 7 × 8 = £56 million (accept 56 000 000)
(f)
[1] Method: 21 × 8760 = 183 960 MWh
[1] 184 GWh (3 s.f.). ECF from (c).

Question 2: Cable-stayed bridge

A bridge has a vertical tower of height 40 m standing on a horizontal deck. One cable runs in a straight line from the top of the tower to a point A on the deck, 55 m horizontally from the base of the tower. A second cable runs from the top of the tower to a point B on the deck on the opposite side of the tower, and makes an angle of 28° with the deck. Cable material costs £340 per metre.

(a) Calculate the length of the cable to A, correct to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the angle the cable to A makes with the deck. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the horizontal distance from the base of the tower to B. (2 marks)
(d) Write down the distance AB along the deck. (1 mark)
(e) The cable to B has length 85.2 m. Verify your answer to (d) by using the cosine rule in the triangle formed by the two cables and the deck. (3 marks)
(f) Calculate the cost of the material for the two cables, to the nearest £100. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: √(40² + 55²) = √4625
[1] 68.0 m (3 s.f.)
Common error: subtracting instead of adding the squares (√1425 = 37.7).
(b)
[1] Method: tan θ = 40 ÷ 55 (or sin θ = 40 ÷ 68.0)
[1] 36.0°
Common error: using 55 ÷ 40 which gives 54.0°.
(c)
[1] Method: tan 28° = 40 ÷ x so x = 40 ÷ tan 28°
[1] 75.2 m (accept 75.23)
Common error: x = 40 × tan 28° = 21.3 m.
(d)
[1] 55 + 75.2 = 130.2 m (accept 130). ECF from (c).
(e)
[1] Angle between the cables at the top of the tower = (90 − 36.0) + (90 − 28) = 116.0° (accept 115.97° or 116°)
[1] Method: AB² = 68.0² + 85.2² − 2 × 68.0 × 85.2 × cos 116.0°
[1] AB = 130.2 m (accept 130), which agrees with (d), so the result is verified. ECF from the angle.
(f)
[1] Method: (68.0 + 85.2) × 340 = £52 088 (accept use of 68.007 and 85.20, giving £52 091)
[1] £52 100 (nearest £100). ECF from (a).

Question 3: Airport terminal floor pattern

The floor of an airport walkway is designed from square tiles. Pattern n has an n by n square of white tiles surrounded by a border of grey tiles, one tile thick.

Pattern 1: 1 white tile and 8 grey tiles.
Pattern 2: 4 white tiles and 12 grey tiles.
Pattern 3: 9 white tiles and 16 grey tiles.

(a) Write down the number of grey tiles in pattern 4. (1 mark)
(b) Find a general rule, in terms of n, for the number of grey tiles in pattern n. (2 marks)
(c) Test your rule by finding the number of grey tiles in pattern 10 using the total number of tiles in the whole pattern minus the number of white tiles. (2 marks)
(d) The whole pattern n is a square with side (n + 2) tiles. Show that (n + 2)² − n² = 4n + 4. (3 marks)
(e) Sam says that one pattern uses exactly 50 grey tiles. Justify whether Sam is correct. (2 marks)
(f) White tiles cost £2.50 each and grey tiles cost £3.20 each. Investigate the largest pattern that can be laid for a budget of £600. Show the cost of the patterns you test. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] 20
(b)
[1] Grey tiles increase by 4 each time, so the rule begins 4n
[1] 4n + 4 (check: n = 1 gives 8). Award 1 mark only for 4n alone.
(c)
[1] Pattern 10: total tiles 12² = 144, white tiles 10² = 100
[1] Grey = 144 − 100 = 44, which matches 4 × 10 + 4 = 44, so the rule is confirmed.
(d)
[1] Expand: (n + 2)² = n² + 4n + 4
[1] Subtract n²: n² + 4n + 4 − n²
[1] = 4n + 4, so the border always has 4n + 4 grey tiles. (Accept a clear algebraic conclusion linking to the rule.)
Common error: writing (n + 2)² = n² + 4 (missing the middle term).
(e)
[1] Solve 4n + 4 = 50 so 4n = 46 and n = 11.5
[1] n is not a whole number, so no pattern has exactly 50 grey tiles and Sam is not correct. ECF from (b).
(f)
[1] Cost formula or method: cost = 2.5 × n² + 3.2 × (4n + 4)
[1] n = 12: cost = 360 + 166.40 = £526.40 (within budget)
[1] n = 13: cost = 422.50 + 179.20 = £601.70 (over budget) so the largest pattern is pattern 12. ECF from (b).

Question 4: Drama club fundraiser

A school drama club sells 240 tickets for a play. Adult tickets cost £8 and child tickets cost £5. The total money raised from tickets is £1560. Let a be the number of adult tickets and c be the number of child tickets.

(a) Write down two equations in a and c. (2 marks)
(b) Solve the equations to find the number of adult tickets sold. (3 marks)

The club also runs a rectangular cake stall. The length of the stall is (x + 3) metres, the width is x metres and the area is 70 m².

(c) Show that x² + 3x − 70 = 0 and solve this equation by factorising to find the width of the stall. (3 marks)

The club sells cakes at £p each. The number of cakes sold is modelled by N = 100 − 5p. Each cake costs £2 to make.

(d) Show that the profit, £P, is given by P = −5p² + 110p − 200. (2 marks)
(e) Determine the price that gives the greatest profit and calculate this profit. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] a + c = 240
[1] 8a + 5c = 1560
(b)
[1] Method: eliminate a variable, e.g. substitute c = 240 − a into 8a + 5c = 1560
[1] 8a + 1200 − 5a = 1560 so 3a = 360
[1] a = 120 adult tickets (check: c = 120 and 960 + 600 = 1560). ECF from (a).
Common error: sign slip when eliminating, giving a = 360 or a = −120.
(c)
[1] Area: x(x + 3) = 70 so x² + 3x = 70, giving x² + 3x − 70 = 0
[1] (x + 10)(x − 7) = 0
[1] x = 7 m (reject x = −10 as a length cannot be negative)
(d)
[1] Profit = (p − 2)(100 − 5p) (revenue minus cost, or profit per cake times number sold)
[1] Expand: 100p − 5p² − 200 + 10p = −5p² + 110p − 200
(e)
[1] Method: complete the square or use the axis of symmetry p = −110 ÷ (2 × −5) = 11
[1] Price = £11
[1] Maximum profit P = −5(121) + 1210 − 200 = £405
Accept a table of values or graphical method with a correct answer. Common error: giving the number of cakes (45) instead of the price.

Question 5: Airport security waiting times

An airport manager records the waiting time, t minutes, of 100 passengers at a security check.

Waiting time (minutes) : number of passengers
0 < t ≤ 10 : 8
10 < t ≤ 20 : 22
20 < t ≤ 30 : x
30 < t ≤ 40 : 25
40 < t ≤ 60 : 10

(a) Show that x = 35. (1 mark)
(b) Write down the modal class. (1 mark)
(c) Estimate the mean waiting time. (3 marks)
(d) Estimate the median waiting time using the cumulative frequencies. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)
(e) Estimate the percentage of passengers who waited longer than 35 minutes. State the assumption you make. (2 marks)
(f) The airport target is that at least 80% of passengers wait 40 minutes or less. Determine whether the target was met. (2 marks)
(g) A second airport reports a mean waiting time of 22.4 minutes and a longest wait of 38 minutes for 100 passengers. Evaluate which airport performs better and give one limitation of your comparison. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] 100 − (8 + 22 + 25 + 10) = 100 − 65 = 35
(b)
[1] 20 < t ≤ 30 (the class with the highest frequency)
(c)
[1] Midpoints 5, 15, 25, 35, 50
[1] Sum of f × midpoint = 40 + 330 + 875 + 875 + 500 = 2620
[1] 2620 ÷ 100 = 26.2 minutes
Common error: using class boundaries instead of midpoints, or dividing by 5 instead of 100.
(d)
[1] The 50th value lies in the class 20 < t ≤ 30 (cumulative frequencies 8, 30, 65, 90, 100)
[1] Interpolation: 20 + (20 ÷ 35) × 10 = 25.7 minutes
(e)
[1] Half of the class 30 < t ≤ 40 plus the last class: 12.5 + 10 = 22.5 passengers, i.e. 22.5%
[1] Assumption: passengers are spread evenly within each class.
(f)
[1] Cumulative frequency up to 40 minutes is 90, i.e. 90%
[1] 90% is at least 80%, so the target was met.
(g)
[1] Second airport has the lower mean (22.4 against 26.2 minutes), so it appears faster on average
[1] Valid justification, e.g. 10 passengers at the first airport waited more than 40 minutes, which is longer than the second airport's longest wait of 38 minutes
[1] Limitation, e.g. only the mean and the longest wait are given, no distribution or median, or the passengers were sampled at different times or days. Accept any sensible limitation.

Question 6: School fair lucky dip

A lucky-dip bag at a school fair contains 10 counters: 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green. A player takes two counters from the bag, one after the other, without replacing the first. A player wins a £5 prize if both counters are the same colour. It costs £2 to play. In total 120 students play.

(a) Write down the probability that the first counter is red. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the probability that both counters are red. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the probability that the two counters are different colours. (3 marks)
(d) Estimate the number of students who win a prize. (2 marks)
(e) The organisers want to make a profit of at least £60 from the lucky dip, after paying out the prizes. Determine, with working, whether they can expect to achieve this. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] 5/10 = 1/2
(b)
[1] Method: 5/10 × 4/9
[1] 20/90 = 2/9
(c)
[1] P(blue, blue) = 3/10 × 2/9 = 6/90 and P(green, green) = 2/10 × 1/9 = 2/90
[1] P(same colour) = 20/90 + 6/90 + 2/90 = 28/90
[1] P(different) = 1 − 28/90 = 62/90 = 31/45
Common error: using replacement, giving 5/10 × 5/10 for red, red.
(d)
[1] Method: 120 × 28/90 (or 120 × 14/45)
[1] 37 students (37.3 accepted). ECF from (c).
(e)
[1] Income 120 × £2 = £240 and expected prizes 37.33 × £5 = £186.67
[1] Expected profit = £240 − £186.67 ≈ £53.33, which is less than £60, so they cannot expect to reach £60. ECF from (d).

Question 7: Electric vehicle charging points

A city had 240 public electric vehicle charging points in 2020. The council models the number of charging points, N, t years after 2020 by N = 240 × 1.18^t, which assumes growth of 18% each year.

(a) Calculate the number of charging points predicted for 2023. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. (2 marks)
(b) Determine, by trial or by solving, the first year in which the model predicts more than 1000 charging points. (3 marks)
(c) In 2025 the council counts 520 charging points. Calculate the percentage error in the model's prediction for 2025, using the counted value as the true value. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
(d) State two assumptions that are made by the model. (2 marks)
(e) The model predicts about 34 400 charging points for 2050. The city has about 200 000 homes. Evaluate the usefulness of the model for long-term planning. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Method: t = 3, N = 240 × 1.18³
[1] 394 charging points (394.3 before rounding)
(b)
[1] Method: test values of t or solve 1.18^t > 1000 ÷ 240
[1] t = 8 gives about 902 (not enough) and t = 9 gives about 1065
[1] First year is 2029
Common error: giving t = 9 without converting to the year.
(c)
[1] Model value for t = 5: 240 × 1.18⁵ = 549.06 (accept 549)
[1] Method: (549.06 − 520) ÷ 520 × 100
[1] 5.6%. Common error: dividing by the model value, giving 5.3%.
(d)
[1] One valid assumption, e.g. the growth rate stays constant at 18% every year
[1] A second valid assumption, e.g. there is no limit on space, funding or demand, or growth is smooth and not affected by policy changes. Accept any two sensible, different assumptions.
(e)
[1] Reasoned comment on accuracy: it is fairly accurate over 5 years (error 5.6%) so is reasonable for short-term use
[1] Limitation: a constant 18% growth cannot realistically continue for 30 years: the number would grow about 143-fold, to about one charging point for every six homes (34 400 ÷ 200 000 ≈ 0.17), with no evidence of demand, space or funding for this
[1] Overall judgement, e.g. use for short-term planning only and update with new counts regularly. ECF from earlier working.

Question 8: Rainwater harvesting at a school

A school plans to collect rainwater from a rectangular roof of length 18 m and width 12.5 m. The yearly rainfall is 640 mm. The system collects 85% of the rain that falls on the roof. The rainwater is stored in a cylindrical tank of radius 1.2 m and height 2.0 m. The school has 600 students, who use 40 litres of water each per school day for toilets. 1 m³ = 1000 litres.

(a) Calculate the volume of rain, in m³, that falls on the roof in a year. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the volume of water collected in a year. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the capacity of the tank in m³, correct to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate how many times the tank could be completely filled in a year. (2 marks)
(e) There are 190 school days in a year. Calculate the percentage of the school's yearly toilet water that the collected rainwater could supply. (3 marks)
(f) A surveyor finds that the true roof area is 231 m². Calculate the percentage error when the roof area is taken as 18 × 12.5. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (2 marks)
(g) The school wants to store enough water for the toilets for one school day, using a cylindrical tank of height 2.0 m. Design the tank by calculating the radius needed, and state one assumption or limitation of your design. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Roof area 18 × 12.5 = 225 m² and rainfall 0.64 m (unit conversion)
[1] 225 × 0.64 = 144 m³
Common error: using 640 without converting from mm to m.
(b)
[1] 0.85 × 144 = 122.4 m³. ECF from (a).
(c)
[1] Method: π × 1.2² × 2.0
[1] 9.05 m³ (3 s.f.)
(d)
[1] Method: 122.4 ÷ 9.05
[1] 13 times (13.5 before rounding down; accept 13 or 'about 13'). ECF from (b) and (c).
(e)
[1] Yearly use = 40 × 600 × 190 = 4 560 000 litres = 4560 m³
[1] Method: 122.4 ÷ 4560 × 100
[1] 2.7% (2.68 before rounding). ECF from (b).
Common error: forgetting to convert litres to m³, giving 0.0027%.
(f)
[1] Method: (231 − 225) ÷ 231 × 100
[1] 2.6%. Accept 2.7% if the error is based on 225 (6 ÷ 225). Award 1 mark for a correct method with a rounding error.
(g)
[1] Daily need 40 × 600 = 24 000 litres = 24 m³
[1] Method: π r² × 2.0 = 24 so r² = 24 ÷ (2π) = 3.82
[1] r = 1.95 m (accept 1.9 to 2.0 m)
[1] Valid assumption or limitation, e.g. every student uses exactly 40 litres, the tank is filled completely, the tank is empty only after one day, or space on site for a tank of diameter 3.9 m is available. Accept any sensible comment.

Question 9: Flight paths from an airport

An aircraft leaves airport A and flies 120 km on a bearing of 070° to a point B. It then turns and flies 90 km on a bearing of 160° to a point C. A second aircraft leaves A and flies 100 km on a bearing of 040° to a point D. Aircraft travel at 450 km/h.

(a) Show that angle ABC = 90°. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the direct distance AC. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the bearing of C from A, to the nearest degree. (3 marks)
(d) The aircraft could have flown directly from A to C. Calculate the distance saved. (1 mark)
(e) Calculate the distance DB, correct to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
(f) Calculate the time taken to fly directly from A to C, in minutes. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] The back bearing from B to A is 070° + 180° = 250°, or use co-interior angles at B
[1] Angle ABC = 250° − 160° = 90°. Accept a clear diagram-based argument using parallel north lines.
(b)
[1] Method: AC² = 120² + 90² (Pythagoras)
[1] AC = 150 km
(c)
[1] Method: tan(BAC) = 90 ÷ 120
[1] BAC = 36.9°
[1] Bearing = 070° + 36.9° = 107° (nearest degree). ECF from the angle.
Common error: subtracting, giving 33°.
(d)
[1] (120 + 90) − 150 = 60 km (the longer route minus the direct route). ECF from (b).
(e)
[1] Angle DAB = 070° − 040° = 30°
[1] Method: DB² = 100² + 120² − 2 × 100 × 120 × cos 30°
[1] DB = 60.1 km (3 s.f.)
(f)
[1] Method: time = 150 ÷ 450 hours = 1/3 hour
[1] 20 minutes. ECF from (b).
